input.text: You've found one of the most unlikely survivals in Beijing: a working astronomical observatory from the Ming dynasty, standing beside the second ring road since fourteen forty-two. For nearly five hundred years, astronomers climbed this platform nightly to track the heavens for the emperor — because in imperial China, the sky was politics: eclipses and comets were omens, and the calendar was the throne's business. The bronze instruments on the roof are the stars of the show — armillary spheres, sextants, and a celestial globe, cast in the late sixteen hundreds under the direction of Ferdinand Verbiest, a Flemish Jesuit priest who served the Kangxi Emperor as court astronomer. Look closely: European engineering wrapped in Chinese dragons and clouds — East and West collaborating three centuries before "globalization". Few visitors find this place; those who do, climb a medieval tower and touch the instruments that once mapped the sky for an empire. Astronomy, diplomacy, and survival — all in one rooftop.
